One-Page High-Yield Summary
General Anesthesia — High-Yield Summary
Anesthesia Pharmacology · Dr. Scott D. Ochs · Mapped to Learning Objectives 1–9
LO1Mechanism of Action & Physiology
  • 3 separate components, not one "off switch": immobility, amnesia, loss of consciousness (LOC) — different drugs, different sites
  • Volatile agents: potentiate GABAA (↑ duration Cl⁻ channel open)
  • N2O: NMDA receptor antagonist (like ketamine) — the mechanistic oddball
  • All: hyperpolarization via K+/Na+ channel effects
  • Immobility site = spinal cord — includes blunting the autonomic reflex spike (HR/BP), not just the flinch
  • Amnesia / LOC site = cortex, brainstem, midbrain; amnesia is already present in Stage I, before LOC
  • Unitary (membrane-expansion) theory = outdated; mechanism today is multi-target, not one site
LO2Theories & Receptor Targets
  • Meyer-Overton hypothesis (unitary/membrane-expansion theory) = outdated; the rule itself (potency ∝ lipid solubility) is still valid
  • Oil:Gas coefficient (measured in olive oil) governs potency; Blood:Gas coefficient governs speed
  • Tight log-log correlation across ~5 orders of magnitude, nitrogen → thiomethoxyflurane
  • Receptor targets: GABAA (volatiles), NMDA (N2O, ketamine)
  • Also: K+/Na+ channel hyperpolarization
  • Current thinking: N2O mainly via NMDA inhibition; volatiles mainly via GABAA potentiation
Oil:Gas × MAC ≈ 1.3
LO3Potency / Class / Duration
AgentMAC%Blood:GasOnsetRecovery
N2O1040.47FastestFast
Halothane0.752.54SlowSlow
Isoflurane1.171.46Interm.Interm.
Desflurane6.60.42Pungency-ltdFastest
Sevoflurane1.80.69Fastest practiceFast
  • Lower Blood:Gas → faster onset and faster recovery (same property, both directions)
  • IV agents = "rapid ultrashort" (propofol/etomidate/ketamine) except thiopental (long w/ infusion)
LO4Inhaled vs. IV/Oral Agents
  • Inhaled: N2O, Halothane not US, Isoflurane rare, Desflurane, Sevoflurane
  • IV: Barbiturates FYI, Propofol, Etomidate, Ketamine, Dexmedetomidine, Benzodiazepines
  • Ketamine: most route-flexible agent — IV, IM, PO, rectal, epidural, intranasal
  • Methohexital: can be given rectally (peds); no sulfur → less fat uptake than thiopental
  • Modern GA is almost never one drug alone — hypnotic + analgesic ± muscle relaxant combo
LO5PK — Onset, Duration, Recovery
  • Inhaled = perfusion-limited, not diffusion-limited (Palv≈Part≈Pbrain) — alveolar membrane is essentially no barrier
  • ↓ Blood:gas solubility → faster onset and faster recovery (pressure builds in alveolus instead of being carried off)
  • ↑ Ventilation or gas flow, or ↓ cardiac output → faster FA/FI rise → faster induction
  • Most volatiles ↓ CO, which self-limits by slightly speeding uptake further; N2O doesn't ↓ CO
  • VRG (brain/liver/kidney) equilibrates almost instantly — small volume, huge perfusion; fat (FG) is the slow reservoir
  • IV = 3-compartment model (V1 central, V2 rapid, V3 depot); effect compartment (ke0) sets onset of effect, separate from CSHT
LO6MAC & Potency
  • MAC = alveolar conc. where 50% don't move to incision (ED50, trapezius squeeze / skin incision)
  • Clinical target = MAC-95 (~1.2–1.3× MAC) — never run at exactly 1.0 MAC
  • MAC-awake 0.3–0.5 (Stage I) · MAC-intubation ~1.3 (tracheal reflex tougher than skin) · MAC-BAR 1.7–2.0 (blocks autonomic response)
  • MAC ↓ with age, hypothermia, other CNS depressants; MAC is additive with N2O (e.g. Iso 1.17 → 0.29 with 60% N2O)
  • ↑ Oil:gas coefficient → ↓ MAC → more potent (Meyer-Overton)
LO7Context-Sensitive Half-Time
  • CSHT = time for plasma conc. to fall 50% after stopping a steady-state infusion
  • ≠ elimination half-life (K10, from the slow terminal phase of a single bolus); CSHT rises with infusion duration (depot tissue loading)
  • Single bolus: rapid drop (→V2) → intermediate (V2↔V3) → slow terminal phase
  • Thiopental = the "hangover" drug — CSHT rises steeply with infusion time
  • Propofol, ketamine, etomidate = CSHT stays low even after long infusion (the "quick recovery" trio)
  • Dexmedetomidine CSHT > propofol's, rises past ~4h before plateauing
LO8Indications / CI / AEs / Interactions
AgentKey AE / CI
N2ODiffusion hypoxia, ↓B12 (megaloblastic anemia >24h); can't use alone (MAC 104%)
HalothaneHepatotox. ("halothane hepatitis"), MH risk (+succinylcholine) → treat with dantrolene
DesfluraneAirway irritation/coughing/laryngospasm >6%; avoid in kids; greenhouse gas
SevofluraneEmergent delirium (peds), Compound A nephrotox. (prevent: fresh gas flow >2 L/min)
BarbituratesCI: acute intermittent porphyria (induce ALA synthase)
Propofol↓BP, egg allergy (intralipid), infusion syndrome (rare, often fatal); antiemetic, no analgesia
EtomidateMyoclonus, 11β-hydroxylase inhibition → adrenal suppression → induction-only, no infusion
KetamineEmergence reactions (adults, not kids); ↑sympathetic tone → preserves BP/CO in trauma
Dexmedetomidine↓/↑BP, bradycardia, sinus arrest; sedation lingers after long infusion
BenzodiazepinesReversed by flumazenil — controlled reversal only, not for OD (seizure risk)
Barbiturate vs. benzo (both bind GABAA): benzos ↑ likelihood GABA opens channel (↑potency, ceiling unchanged); barbiturates ↑ duration open, can be direct agonists at high dose — more dangerous.
LO9Application & Patient Monitoring
  • Consciousness check = trapezius squeeze
  • Guedel stages: I Analgesia → II Excitement/delirium → III Surgical anesthesia (4 planes; targets plane 3) → IV Medullary depression/overdose
  • Stage II can reappear on emergence — classic with sevoflurane (peds) or ketamine (adults)
  • Color-coded vaporizers: Sevo=yellow, Des=blue, Iso=purple; Des vaporizer is a distinct heated unit (prevents mix-ups)
  • Balanced anesthesia: hypnotic + analgesic ± muscle relaxant → less of each drug needed
  • 5 goals: unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, ↓autonomic reflex, muscle relaxation — no single agent covers all 5 safely alone
  • MH treatment = dantrolene; flumazenil = controlled reversal only (not for benzo OD)
Overview

General Anesthesia — Definition & History

General anesthesia is a drug-induced, reversible state with three distinct physiologic goals — not a single "off switch" for the brain. Understanding which drug hits which target is the foundation for everything that follows: mechanism, potency, pharmacokinetics, and clinical use.

The Three Components

🧍
Component 1
Immobility
A nonrelaxed patient stays still at the moment of incision — this includes blunting the autonomic reflex response (no reflex spike in heart rate or blood pressure to the cut), not just the physical flinch.
🌫️
Component 2
Amnesia
Prevents formation of both explicit and implicit memories. Amnesia is already present in Stage I — before the patient ever loses consciousness.
😴
Component 3
Loss of Consciousness
Loss of awareness, wakefulness, and perception. Philosophically tricky: you can't truly prove unconsciousness, because amnesia erases any memory of having been aware.
🧠 Memory Hook
Anesthesia isn't one "off switch" for the brain — it's three separate switches, hit by drugs acting at different sites (spinal cord for immobility; cortex/brainstem for amnesia and consciousness). That's why a paralyzed patient can still need anesthetic depth monitoring, and why amnesia can outlast the memory of ever "waking up."
👶 ELI5
Imagine three dimmer switches, not one: Move (can you flinch?), Remember (will you recall the pain?), and Aware (are the lights on upstairs?). General anesthesia turns all three down together — but they don't dim at the same rate, which is why amnesia can kick in before you're technically "asleep."

Drugs Used During General Anesthesia

Today's focus

  • Hypnotics — induce unconsciousness (inhaled gases + most IV agents)

Covered briefly / elsewhere

  • Analgesics — analgesia + hemodynamic suppression (opioids, covered under Balanced Anesthesia)
  • Muscle relaxants — suppress reflex movement (neuromuscular blockers — separate lecture)
⚠️ Board framing
Modern general anesthesia is almost never one drug alone — it's a combination of hypnotic, analgesic, and (when needed) muscle-relaxant agents. Keep this in mind every time a question asks "which single agent would you use."

General Anesthetic Agents at a Glance

Inhaled gases

  • Nitrous Oxide (N2O)
  • Halothane not used in US
  • Isoflurane rarely used
  • Desflurane
  • Sevoflurane

Intravenous agents

  • Barbiturates FYI only
  • Etomidate
  • Propofol
  • Ketamine
  • Dexmedetomidine
Pharmacokinetics

Pharmacokinetics of Inhaled Anesthetics

Everything about inhaled anesthetic speed comes down to one variable: how fast you can raise the alveolar partial pressure.

Absorption — It's All About Alveolar Pressure

Diffusion rate = D × (A / l) × ΔP

The alveolar surface area (A) is enormous and the membrane thickness (l) is negligible — so diffusion across the alveolar membrane is essentially instantaneous. That means Palv ≈ Part ≈ Pbrain at nearly all times. Inhaled anesthetics are therefore perfusion-limited, not diffusion-limited — the bottleneck isn't crossing the membrane, it's how much drug the blood carries away.

↑ Ventilation rate → ↑ Alveolar partial pressure → Faster anesthesia
↓ Rate of absorption into blood → ↑ Alveolar partial pressure → Faster anesthesia (low blood solubility → pressure builds up in the alveolus instead of being carried off)

Partition Coefficients

A partition coefficient is a ratio describing how the anesthetic distributes between two phases at equilibrium (equal partial pressures in both phases).

🩸
Blood : Gas coefficient
Governs speed
A coefficient of 0.5 means blood concentration is half the alveolar concentration at equal partial pressures — the drug isn't very soluble in blood, so pressure builds up fast in the alveolar space. Counterintuitively, poor blood solubility = faster onset.
🫙
Oil : Gas coefficient
Governs potency
Measured empirically in olive oil. Correlates with lipid solubility and therefore potency (Meyer-Overton), not onset. Higher oil:gas coefficient → lower MAC → more potent.
⚠️ High-yield relationship
Speed and potency are usually inversely related. Nitrous oxide is the fastest-onset agent and the least potent. Halothane is the most potent and among the slowest.
👶 ELI5
Think of the alveolus as a small waiting room and the blood as a bus that carries drug away. If the drug barely dissolves in blood (low blood:gas), the "bus" only takes a few passengers each trip — so the waiting room (alveolar pressure) fills up fast, and the brain equilibrates fast too. If the drug loves blood (high blood:gas), the bus fills to capacity every trip and keeps carrying drug away, so the waiting room takes forever to pressurize.
🧠 Memory Hook
Low solubility, fast mobility. Poor blood solubility = fast onset AND fast recovery (same property drives both directions) — that's N2O, desflurane, sevoflurane. High solubility (halothane) = slow onset, slow "hangover."

Rate of Onset and Recovery: FA/FI

FA = alveolar fractional concentration. FI = inspired fractional concentration. The faster FA/FI approaches 1, the faster the onset. The least soluble drugs (lowest blood:gas coefficient) have both the fastest onset and the fastest recovery — same underlying property drives both directions. N2O, desflurane, and sevoflurane are considered perfusion-limited anesthetics.

Figure FA/FI rate-of-onset curves across the major inhaled agents Course lecture slides
Gotcha
This classic graph always shows N2O with the fastest onset — but N2O isn't the lowest blood:gas coefficient in the group. It's dosed at a much higher inspired concentration (up to 70–104%) than the potent volatile agents (~1–8%), so the comparison isn't apples-to-apples.

Uptake Model — Tissue Compartments

Tissues are grouped by perfusion and anesthetic capacity:

GroupTissues% Cardiac Output% Body Weight
VRGBrain, liver, kidneys75%9%
MGMuscle, skin18%50%
FGFat5.5%19%
VPGBone, cartilage, ligament1.5%22%
Figure VRG / MG / FG / VPG — perfusion and anesthetic volume capacity by tissue group Course lecture slides (Golan, Principles of Pharmacology)

Because the vessel-rich group gets most of the cardiac output but has the lowest volume capacity, it equilibrates almost as fast as the blood does. Once alveolar and arterial pressures equilibrate, the brain is right behind — there's essentially no lag between blood and brain equilibration.

🧠 Memory Hook
Line the four groups up by how fast they fill and how big they are: VRG = small tank, huge hose (brain/liver/kidneys — equilibrates almost instantly). MG = medium tank, medium hose (muscle/skin — takes longer). FG = huge tank, thin hose (fat — a slow-filling reservoir that matters most on long cases). VPG = tiny tank, barely any hose (bone/cartilage — essentially irrelevant to onset).

Elimination

Tissue depots have little effect on arterial anesthetic concentration for inhaled agents — most current drugs have low blood:gas coefficients, so they clear straight out through the lungs before they ever meaningfully load peripheral tissue.

Contrast to remember
This is the exact opposite situation from IV anesthetics, where tissue depot loading is central to the concept of context-sensitive half-time (see the IV Pharmacokinetics section below).

Factors Influencing Speed of Action

FactorEffect on Speed
Inspired (FI) partial pressure↑ FI → faster induction
Gas flow rate↑ flow → faster circuit turnover → faster induction
Alveolar (FA) partial pressureControls anesthetic partial pressure in all body tissues
Anesthetic solubility↑ solubility → slower FA/FI rise → slower onset
Ventilation↑ ventilation → faster FA/FI rise
Cardiac output↓ CO → faster FA/FI rise (less blood around to carry drug away)
Self-limiting loop
Nearly all inhaled agents suppress cardiac output — which, per the table above, would slightly speed up further uptake. It's a small effect, but it's there. Nitrous oxide is the exception — it does not suppress cardiac output.
Depth of Anesthesia

Stages & Measuring Anesthesia

Guedel's Four Stages

Figure Guedel's four stages of anesthesia — deepening (left) and recovery (right) Course lecture slides
I
Stage I
Analgesia
Analgesia (agent-dependent), amnesia already present, still conscious. This is where conscious sedation and N2O-alone procedures live — MAC-awake.
II
Stage II
Excitement
Excitement, delirium, combative behavior. Usually blown through quickly on induction — but can show up on emergence, classically with sevoflurane (esp. children) or ketamine.
III
Stage III
Surgical Anesthesia
Unconsciousness, regular respiration, decreasing eye movement. Has 4 planes — general surgery typically targets plane 3.
IV
Stage IV
Medullary Depression
Overdose/toxicity. Respiratory arrest → cardiac depression/arrest → death. Must avoid.
Recovery from anesthesia moves back through these same stages in reverse.
🧠 Memory Hook
"Aware, Awful, Asleep-for-surgery, Arrest." Stage I you're still aware (just numb/amnestic). Stage II is the awful, thrashing excitement phase. Stage III is where surgery actually happens. Stage IV means you've gone too deep — it's an overdose, not a destination.

Measuring Depth — MAC

Consciousness can be checked with the trapezius squeeze test. But the core quantitative concept is minimum alveolar concentration (MAC): the alveolar partial pressure at which 50% of patients do not respond to a surgical incision — essentially the ED50 for inhaled anesthetics.

⚠️ Board pearl
You would never run surgery at exactly 1.0 MAC — half your patients would move. Clinically, surgery targets MAC-95, roughly 1.2–1.3× MAC.
👶 ELI5
MAC is basically a "coin-flip dose" — the concentration where a coin flip decides whether the patient moves when cut. It's the anesthesia version of an ED50, and just like any ED50, you dose above it in practice so you're not gambling on half your patients.
Figure Dose-response curves: non-response to trapezius squeeze, skin incision, intubation, and LP50 (cardiac arrest) Course lecture slides
🎯
MAC-intubation
~1.3 MAC
Concentration needed to prevent movement/coughing with intubation — the tracheal reflex is tougher to suppress than a skin incision.
🚫
MAC-BAR
1.7–2.0 MAC
Blocks the autonomic response (BAR = blocks autonomic response) to noxious stimuli — total loss of reflex, usually slightly higher than MAC-intubation.
💤
MAC-awake
0.3–0.5 MAC
Concentration at which patients stop responding to questions and lose perceptive awareness — functionally, Stage I.

How to read this table
Given this table, you should be able to answer: which drug has the fastest onset (lowest blood/gas coefficient)? Which is most potent (lowest MAC, highest oil/gas coefficient)? Notice N2O has the highest MAC (least potent) and the lowest oil/gas coefficient — potency measures line up together, as expected from Meyer-Overton.

MAC decreases with age, hypothermia, and concurrent use of CNS depressants/other anesthetics.

Mechanism

Meyer-Overton & Mechanism of Action

Meyer-Overton Hypothesis outdated

Over a century old: the unitary theory of anesthesia — a single biological site of action, where anesthetics alter neurotransmission by causing expansion or fluidization of the plasma membrane. No longer accepted.

Meyer-Overton Rule still valid

Potency increases with lipid solubility. This correlation is the Meyer-Overton constant:

Oil/Gas Partition Coefficient × MAC ≈ 1.3

Given one variable, back-calculate the other by dividing by 1.3.

👶 ELI5
Anesthetic molecules that are more "fat-loving" (lipophilic) are more potent — the oilier the drug, the less of it you need. That's why an oil-loving vodka analogy works: a drug that dissolves easily into fatty membranes gets into the brain's lipid bilayer more efficiently, so a smaller partial pressure does the job. Oily = potent, low MAC.
Figure Potency vs. oil/gas partition coefficient — a tight log-log correlation spanning five orders of magnitude, from nitrogen to thiomethoxyflurane Course lecture slides

Mechanism of Action: UNKNOWN (as a single mechanism)

The unitary theory is out, but the Meyer-Overton correlation itself is still valid — so what's actually happening at the receptor level? Evidence supports several specific molecular targets:

  • Potentiation of GABAA receptors
  • Inhibition of glutamate (NMDA) receptors — including nitrous oxide
  • Hyperpolarization of the membrane via K+ and Na+ channel effects
Current thinking
The nonvolatile gas N2O most likely works mainly through NMDA receptor inhibition, while the volatile halogenated agents work mainly through GABAA potentiation.
🧠 Memory Hook
N2O is the oddball everywhere in this lecture — different mechanism (NMDA, like ketamine), no cardiovascular depression, and it can't be used alone. If a question describes the "exception," it's almost always N2O.

Site of Action

Immobility

Site of action: spinal cord

Amnesia & Loss of Consciousness

Site of action: brainstem, midbrain, and cerebral cortex

Individual Agents

Individual Inhaled Agents

Board-relevant details for each agent — remember most of these are used in combination, not alone.

Nitrous Oxide (N2O) — "No Laughing Matter"

  • Causes diffusion hypoxia during recovery
  • Sympathetic stimulation prevents the fall in arterial pressure that the other volatile agents show — this is why N2O is the outlier on nearly every hemodynamic comparison
  • Has analgesic properties, thought to involve α2B-adrenergic receptor agonism in the descending pain pathway
  • No smell, no taste — well tolerated, commonly used in children (e.g., dental procedures with a local anesthetic)
  • Cannot be used alone for induction — it's too weak (MAC of 104% — not physically achievable)
Adverse effects
Inhibits vitamin B12–dependent enzymes → risk of hematopoietic dysfunction (megaloblastic anemia with prolonged use, e.g., >24h) and neurologic dysfunction (seen with chronic recreational abuse — mechanism overlaps with ketamine's NMDA antagonism).
🧠 Memory Hook
N2O keeps breaking the pattern: no BP drop (direct sympathetic stimulation), no reflex tachycardia, NMDA (not GABA) mechanism, and it can't be used alone (MAC of 104% is physically impossible to deliver). One gas, four exceptions.

Halothane

  • On the WHO Essential Medicines List — inexpensive, still used internationally (especially in developing countries), not available in the US
  • Can be used for inhalation-only induction; well tolerated in children (thymol preservative gives it a sweet odor)
Adverse effects
Hepatotoxicity ("halothane hepatitis") and increased risk of malignant hyperthermia (very high fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, acidosis, muscle rigidity, rhabdomyolysis) — risk rises further when combined with succinylcholine. Treat malignant hyperthermia with dantrolene.
🧠 Memory Hook
"Ha-LIVER-thane." Halothane hits the liver (hepatotoxicity) and, paired with succinylcholine, can trigger a fire the body can't put out (malignant hyperthermia) — the antidote is dantrolene, full stop, memorize that pairing cold.

Desflurane

  • Fastest rate of recovery (lowest tissue/blood solubility) — but not the fastest onset in practice
  • Concentrations >6% cause coughing, breath-holding, laryngospasm, and salivation — premedicate with opioids to blunt this
  • Very pungent — do not use in children (also carries emergent delirium risk, just masked because it isn't used pediatrically)
  • Requires a complex heated vaporizer
  • Significant greenhouse gas effect — being pushed out of the market for both airway-irritation and environmental reasons
🧠 Memory Hook
Des = "distasteful." Fastest recovery on paper, but too pungent to breathe down comfortably — so it's the recovery champion, not the induction champion. That title goes to sevoflurane.

Sevoflurane

  • Fastest rate of induction in practice (low solubility + low pungency, no concentration ceiling like desflurane)
  • Can be used for inhalation-only induction; causes bronchodilation
  • Preferred over desflurane in children
  • N2O does not speed up sevoflurane induction and may cause excitation — unlike isoflurane/desflurane, don't bother combining N2O with sevoflurane
Adverse effects
Emergent delirium in pediatric patients (mirror image of ketamine, which tends to spare kids from emergence reactions). Nephrotoxicity via Compound A, which forms in desiccated soda lime — maintain fresh gas flow >2 L/min to prevent it. In practice this is low-risk because modern machines use agent-specific vaporizers.
🧠 Memory Hook
Sevo = Smooth. Low pungency + no concentration ceiling = the go-to inhalation induction agent, especially in kids. Trade-off: kids who go smoothly to sleep sometimes wake up rough (emergent delirium) — the opposite of ketamine's pattern.

Systemic Effects

Systemic Effects & Administration

Volatile Gases Decrease Mean Arterial Pressure

Figure % awake blood pressure and % awake cardiac output vs. anesthetic dose (MAC units) Course lecture slides

Desflurane and isoflurane show the greatest blood-pressure-lowering effect; sevoflurane the least among the volatiles. N2O has minimal effect and isn't shown on this chart.

Additional Effects

Figure Systemic effects of volatile anesthetics by organ system (CBF, ICP, RR, TV, PaCO2, CO, CVP, HBF, RBF, GFR, BP, SVR) Course lecture slides
🫁
Respiratory rate
All ↑ RR, dose-dependently
↓ tidal volume → ↑ PaCO2 → compensatory tachypnea (for the volatiles; N2O's tachypnea may reflect direct CNS stimulation instead, since it barely affects tidal volume).
❤️
Heart rate
All ↑ HR — except N2O
Baroreceptor reflex to falling BP. N2O doesn't drop BP (direct sympathetic stimulation), so no reflex tachycardia.
💔
Contractility
All negative inotropes — except N2O
N2O does cause direct myocardial depression, but its direct sympathetic activation offsets the observable effect.
💪
Skeletal muscle
All relax skeletal muscle — except N2O
Useful — lets you reduce the dose of neuromuscular blocker needed.
🧠 Memory Hook
Four systemic effects, one exception each time: all volatiles ↑RR, ↑HR, ↓contractility, and relax muscle — except N2O, which does none of that because it drives sympathetic tone up instead of blood pressure down. If you see "the odd one out," bet on nitrous.

IV Pharmacokinetics

Intravenous Anesthetics — Pharmacokinetics

The Three-Compartment Model

Most IV anesthetics are best represented by a 3-compartment model. Unlike inhaled agents, IV drugs are injected directly into the venous side — they have to circulate through the lungs to the arterial side before reaching their site of action (the brain).

Figure Three-compartment model with an added effect-site compartment Course lecture slides
Figure Plasma concentration after a single bolus — rapid (red), intermediate (blue), slow terminal (green) phases Course lecture slides
🩺
V1
Central compartment
Systemic circulation + highly vessel-rich tissues (brain, heart). Loads first since the drug is injected straight in.
⚡
V2
Rapidly equilibrating
Fills quickly after the initial bolus — responsible for the fast early drop in plasma concentration.
🐢
V3
Slowly equilibrating (depot)
Takes much longer to fill and empty — this is the "storage depot" that drives context-sensitive half-time.

After a single bolus: an almost instantaneous rapid drop (redistribution into V2) → an intermediate phase (V2↔V3 equilibrating, some clearance) → a slow log-linear terminal phase — this terminal phase is the one used to calculate a textbook elimination half-life (K10).

Effect compartment
A separate, negligible-volume compartment connected by rate constant ke0 — this is what actually determines onset of drug effect. It is a completely separate concept from context-sensitive half-time.

Context-Sensitive Half-Time

Definition: the time for plasma concentration to fall 50% after stopping an infusion that had maintained a steady-state concentration. This is not the same as elimination half-life, and it increases with longer infusion duration because of drug accumulation in peripheral (depot) tissue.

Figure Context-sensitive half-time vs. infusion duration — fentanyl, thiopental, midazolam, sufentanil, alfentanil, propofol Hughes, Glass, Jacobs — Anesthesiology 1992
Why some drugs "hang over" and others don't
A single bolus drops 50% almost instantly (rapid redistribution into V2). A long infusion loads V1, V2, and V3 near equilibrium — so when you stop, the depot tissue keeps feeding drug back into V1, and blood levels barely fall. Thiopental is the poster child (long infusion → very long CSHT, the classic anesthesia "hangover" drug). Propofol, ketamine, and etomidate stay comparatively low even after prolonged infusions.

Clinical translation: CSHT tells you how long the anesthetic effect will linger once you stop the infusion — critical for planning emergence and recovery, and it cannot be predicted from elimination half-life alone.

👶 ELI5
Picture a bathtub with the drain wide open. A quick splash of water (single bolus) drains to half-full almost instantly. But if you've been running the faucet for hours (long infusion), the tub — and the sponge sitting in it (peripheral tissue) — are both soaked, so even with the same size drain, it takes much longer to get back to half-full. The drain never changed; how long you ran the faucet did.
🧠 Memory Hook
Thiopental = the hangover drug. Its CSHT rises steeply with infusion time — that's the pharmacologic reason "truth serum" leaves patients groggy for hours. Propofol, ketamine, and etomidate are the "quick recovery" trio precisely because their CSHT stays flat even after a long infusion.
IV Agents

Individual IV Agents

Barbiturates FYI

Both largely replaced clinically by propofol — included for completeness.

FYI Thiopental — the classic "truth serum" barbiturate Course lecture slides

Thiopental

Rapid, ultrashort-acting. MOA: potentiates GABAA (Cl- channel) by increasing duration of opening; may act as a direct agonist at higher concentrations; also attenuates excitatory glutamate transmission at AMPA receptors. Contraindication: acute intermittent porphyria. AEs: respiratory depression, apnea.

Methohexital

Rapid ultrashort-acting; no sulfur → reduced uptake into fat. Repeated boluses/infusion cause a more marked decrease in elimination than thiopental. Same MOA, contraindication, and AEs as thiopental. Can be given rectally.

🧠 Memory Hook
"Barb-iturates block Bathroom breaks." Contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria because they induce ALA synthase and can precipitate a life-threatening attack — a classic single-fact board trap.

Propofol

Rapid, ultrashort-acting IV anesthetic. MOA not fully understood — binds the β subunit of the GABAA receptor (non-interface site), potentiating its activity.

Figure Propofol — the classic white intralipid emulsion Course lecture slides
Intralipid formulation — two things to remember
(1) Handled sloppily, it's a good bacterial growth medium — a rare but real source of infection. (2) In a critically ill patient on a long infusion, it's a genuine caloric source — dietitians need to know so they can adjust TPN lipid content. Can also cause hypertriglyceridemia.
  • Indications: most frequently used induction agent; also maintenance, monitored anesthesia care, conscious sedation
  • Contraindication: egg allergy (the lipid emulsion is egg-derived)
  • PK: short context-sensitive half-time → prompt recovery even after prolonged infusion
  • AEs: hypotension, respiratory depression, injection-site pain, rare infection, cloudy/green urine discoloration, rare propofol infusion syndrome (long-term critical-care infusion → cardiac failure, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, hyperkalemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hepatomegaly — often fatal)
  • Bonus: antiemetic effect
Fospropofol
A water-soluble prodrug, converted to propofol by alkaline phosphatase — not an intralipid formulation (so no egg-allergy or infection-risk concern).
🧠 Memory Hook
"Milk of amnesia." White, egg-based emulsion, egg-allergy contraindication, and a short CSHT that makes it the default induction and MAC/sedation workhorse — but remember, it treats nausea, not pain (no analgesic effect).

Etomidate

Rapid, ultrashort-acting IV anesthetic. MOA not fully understood — binds β2- or β3-subunit-containing GABAA receptors (transmembrane interface site), potentiating activity.

Figure GABA-A receptor subunits and binding sites (benzodiazepine, barbiturate, ethanol, neurosteroid) Course lecture slides
  • Indication: rapid induction of anesthesia only — cannot be given as a continuous infusion
  • Minimal cardiovascular and respiratory effects → wide margin of safety, useful for hemodynamically unstable patients needing intubation
Adverse effects
Myoclonus and injection-site pain. Inhibits 11β-hydroxylase (also 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase and the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme) → suppresses cortisol and aldosterone synthesis → risk of adrenal insufficiency. This is exactly why it's induction-only.
Flip side
That same steroidogenesis inhibition could, in theory, make etomidate useful perioperatively in a patient with an excess-steroid-hormone state.
🧠 Memory Hook
"Etomidate: easy on the heart, hard on the adrenals." Minimal hemodynamic effects make it the pick for unstable patients needing intubation — but adrenal suppression (11β-hydroxylase inhibition) is exactly why it's induction-only, never an infusion.

Ketamine — "A Special Anesthetic"

A phencyclidine (PCP) derivative, originally a veterinary anesthetic, now heavily used in emergency medicine. Produces a "dissociative anesthetic" state — eyes remain open with a slow nystagmic gaze, a "cataleptic state." MOA: NMDA receptor uncompetitive antagonist (binds inside the open channel pore, not an allosteric site).

💉
Effects
Analgesia + ↑ sympathetic tone
Significant analgesia, increased sympathetic outflow → increased cardiac output, bronchodilation, minimal respiratory depression.
🚑
Why the ER loves it
Preserves hemodynamics
Ideal for hemodynamically unstable trauma patients — you don't want to drop their blood pressure further.
🧒
Pediatrics
Fewer emergence reactions in kids
Opposite pattern from sevoflurane's pediatric emergence delirium — a good pediatric ER choice.
  • Indications: induction, adjunct during general anesthesia (especially when preserved cardiac output matters); can be given IV, IM, oral, rectal, epidural, or intranasally
  • AEs: unpleasant emergence reactions in adults (hallucinations, out-of-body experiences, psychedelia)
👶 ELI5
Ketamine "disconnects" the brain rather than shutting it off — eyes stay open, the patient looks awake but isn't processing normally (dissociative anesthesia), like the brain's wires got unplugged from each other instead of powered down.
🧠 Memory Hook
Ketamine is the anti-propofol. Propofol drops BP and gives no analgesia; ketamine raises BP (sympathetic surge) and gives strong analgesia. That's why it's the trauma/hemodynamically-unstable-patient favorite — and why kids tolerate emergence better than adults do (opposite of sevoflurane's pediatric pattern).

Dexmedetomidine

A very selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist — think of it as clonidine's CNS-selective cousin.

Figure Locus coeruleus / VLPO sleep circuitry — awake state vs. NREM sleep Course lecture slides

Hypnotic effect

Inhibits the locus coeruleus (noradrenergic neurons) → disinhibits the VLPO (ventrolateral preoptic nucleus, the brain's sleep-initiating center) → increased VLPO activity → sleep state.

Analgesic effect

Stimulates α2 receptors in the descending pain pathway in the spinal cord — the same general strategy as N2O's analgesic mechanism.

Figure Context-sensitive half-time — dexmedetomidine vs. propofol, ketamine, midazolam, thiopental, fentanyl Course lecture slides
  • PK: rapid hepatic metabolism, minimal excretion as unchanged drug; elimination half-life 2–3 hours; context-sensitive half-time longer than propofol's, rising steeply past ~4 hours of infusion before plateauing
  • Indication: sedation for intubated/mechanically ventilated ICU patients ("fighting the ventilator") — given by infusion because of the short elimination half-life, but sedation lingers well after a long infusion is stopped (unlike propofol)
  • AEs: hypotension, transient hypertension, bradycardia, sinus arrest, respiratory depression
👶 ELI5
Dexmedetomidine borrows the brain's own "go to sleep" switch (the same circuit that drives natural NREM sleep) instead of forcing unconsciousness — that's why patients on it are sedated but easily rousable, more like a nap than a coma.
🧠 Memory Hook
Dexmedetomidine is clonidine's CNS-selective cousin — α2 agonism gives both sedation (via locus coeruleus) and analgesia (via the spinal cord), the same descending-pathway trick N2O uses for its own analgesia.

Benzodiazepines

Agents: diazepam, lorazepam, and midazolam (most commonly used in this context — faster onset, greater amnesia, less postoperative sedation than the others).

  • Indication: preoperative sedation — anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia, given 15–60 minutes before induction; can be part of a general anesthesia regimen
  • MOA: binds the benzodiazepine site on GABAA receptors
  • Minimal respiratory depression
Benzodiazepine vs. barbiturate — the key distinction
Both bind GABAA, but differently. Benzodiazepines increase the likelihood that endogenous GABA opens the channel — they shift the GABA dose-response curve leftward (↑ potency) without raising the ceiling (efficacy stays the same, no matter the dose). Barbiturates increase the duration the channel stays open (↑ efficacy) and can act as direct agonists at high dose — which is exactly why they carry more danger and more respiratory depression than benzodiazepines.
👶 ELI5
Think of the GABAA channel as a door with an endogenous doorman (GABA). Benzodiazepines just make the doorman more likely to let people through — they can't force the door open by themselves. Barbiturates prop the door open longer every time, and at high enough doses can shove it open on their own — which is why an overdose is so much more dangerous.
Reversal — flumazenil
A benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. Do not give it for a benzodiazepine overdose — risk of precipitating seizures. Its real use is a controlled reversal after a large intraoperative benzodiazepine load, in a monitored setting where the dose given is known.
🧠 Memory Hook
Midazolam = the "M&A" drug — fast onset, strong anterograde Amnesia, minimal respiratory depression, and reversible with flumazenil (but only in a controlled setting, never blindly for an overdose).
Clinical Application

Balanced Anesthesia

No single general anesthetic checks every box safely at a tolerable dose — that's the whole reason modern anesthesia combines drug classes. (Opioids are analgesic-only adjuncts, not anesthetics themselves — they don't cause amnesia or unconsciousness alone — but they're the classic partner that lets you use less of the general anesthetic.)

Five desired effects — the whole point of combining agents is that you need less of each drug to hit all five safely:

😴
Goal 1
Unconsciousness
Inhaled anesthetics, sedative-hypnotics
🌫️
Goal 2
Amnesia
Inhaled anesthetics, sedative-hypnotics
💊
Goal 3
Analgesia
Opioids, inhaled anesthetics, and select IV agents (N2O, ketamine, dexmedetomidine)
🛑
Goal 4
Inhibition of autonomic reflexes
Inhaled anesthetics, opioids
💪
Goal 5
Skeletal muscle relaxation
Inhaled anesthetics, neuromuscular blockers
Don't forget
Propofol does not contribute analgesia — its "bonus" effect is antiemetic, not analgesic. If a question implies propofol alone is covering pain control, that's a trap.
🧠 Memory Hook
"Balanced" means a team, not a hero drug. Every agent in this lecture earns its spot on the balanced anesthesia roster by covering one or two of the five goals — knowing which drug covers which goal is really just this whole lecture, restated as a checklist.
